text: A personal web app for one person to keep track of money coming in and going out, without typing every record by hand.

You upload a bank transfer slip or photograph a bill. The app reads the image with Claude (an AI that can read pictures) and fills in the amount, currency, date, who was paid, whether it was income or spending, and a category.
You check the result, fix anything wrong and save it. The app then adds everything up and shows totals as charts.
Slips and bills can be in Thai or English, and amounts can be in more than one currency.

stories.want: to upload a bank slip image and get a pre-filled record I can confirm in one click
criteria: Accepts photos in the common formats (JPEG, PNG, WebP and HEIC) up to 10 MB.
Reads the details within 15 seconds for a typical slip. If something cannot be read, that field is left empty and marked, and nothing is saved silently.
A record made by the AI is saved only after you confirm it. The original image stays linked to the record so you can view it later.
A receipt with several items becomes one record with the total amount and one category.
Each record keeps its original amount and currency, plus its value in Thai baht (THB).
For money in another currency, the app looks up that day's exchange rate from a free service, shows it in the form and lets you change it. If the lookup fails, you must type a rate before saving.
Dates show in the Western calendar, for example 14 Oct 2026. Years in the Thai Buddhist calendar printed on slips are converted.
If a new record has the same amount, date and slip reference number as an existing one, the app warns you before saving.

stories.want: to take a photo of a paper bill on my phone and get the same pre-filled record
criteria: On a phone, choosing a file also offers the camera.
The app works on a small phone screen and on a desktop screen.

stories.want: to add a record by hand when I have no image
criteria: Every field the AI fills in can also be typed in and edited by hand.

stories.want: to edit or delete any record, including ones the AI created
criteria: Every saved record can be edited or deleted. Deleting asks you to confirm.
Ready-made categories exist for spending and for income. You can add, rename and remove categories, but a category that is in use cannot be removed until its records are moved.

stories.want: to see where my money went this month in a category chart, and how income compares with expenses over time
criteria: For a chosen period (the current month by default), the app shows total income, total spending and the difference, all in THB.
A ring-shaped chart shows spending by category, and a bar chart compares income with spending for each of the last 6 months, all in THB.

stories.want: to filter records by date range, category, direction and currency
criteria: Both charts follow the filters you set.

stories.want: to export all my records to a spreadsheet file (CSV) as a backup
criteria: One button downloads all records, or only the filtered ones, as a file that opens correctly in Excel, including Thai text.

stack.plain: A popular toolkit for building web apps. TypeScript is a stricter form of JavaScript that catches mistakes early.
The program that runs the app on your PC.
A database stored in one file on your computer.
An AI that can read pictures. It pulls the details out of a slip or bill.
A free online service that gives daily exchange rates.
A checker that makes sure information is complete and sensible before it is saved.
Draws the charts on the dashboard.
A tool for styling the screens in a consistent way.
Converts iPhone photos to a common format and shrinks large images before they are sent to the AI.
Tools that test the app automatically: one checks small pieces, the other uses the app like a person would.

always: Run the automatic checks before every save of the code.
Check all input and all AI answers before they touch the database.
Keep the AI key private on the server.
Store money as whole numbers of the smallest coin (such as satang), never as decimals.
Check for secrets and personal data before every upload to the public code site.

decisions.text: All totals and charts are in THB. Other currencies are converted with a rate from a free service, which you can override.
Dates are shown in the Western calendar. Thai Buddhist years on slips are converted when the slip is read.
Phase 1 has no login and runs on your home network only. Phase 2 adds a single-password login because the app becomes public.
Phase 1 runs on your PC. Phase 2 puts the app on your Railway account with the database on a storage volume.
A receipt becomes one record with the total amount only.
Backup is a manual export button (CSV).
Phase 2 login is a single password kept for 30 days. No Google sign-in and no two-step verification.
Phase 2 uses the free Railway web address, not a custom domain.
Saving changes goes through its own entry points, so it can be tested without the screens and reused when the app goes online.
Each kind of record has one set of checking rules, shared by the form, the saving step and the AI answer reader.
Money is stored as whole numbers of the smallest coin and rates as exact decimal text. The THB amount comes from one function that rounds half up.
All file locations come from one setting, so going online only changes a setting.
The AI reading step sits behind one function. Tests use a stand-in, and only a manual command calls the real AI.
Claude is asked for its answer in a fixed format, and any field it leaves out is flagged for you to fill in.
Dates are stored as Western-calendar dates. Thai Buddhist years are converted only when a slip is read.
Filters live in the web address, so the list, dashboard and export share them and links can be bookmarked.
Colours and text sizes are set once in Task 5 and reused everywhere, which avoids a restyle at the end.
You add real slips and bills to a private folder that is not uploaded: 3 to 5 before Task 2 and about 10 by Checkpoint D.
You already have an API key and paste it into the private settings file at Task 2. The price per image is checked before the first paid run.

success.text: From a phone on your home network, you can photograph a bill and save a correct record in under 30 seconds, including the review.
On 10 sample slips and bills (Thai and English), the AI gets amount, currency and date right in at least 9, and suggests a sensible category in at least 8. Mistakes can be fixed in the review form.
Adding, changing and deleting records and categories all work, and the data is still there after a restart.
The dashboard totals in THB match a hand calculation on test data, including records in other currencies.
A Thai slip dated in the Buddhist calendar is saved and shown with the correct Western date.
The CSV export opens in Excel with Thai text intact, and the THB amounts match the dashboard.
All automatic checks pass and at least 80% of the core code is covered by tests.
No secrets or personal data appear anywhere in the code history.
The app is live on a secure Railway address, and you can photograph a bill on mobile data and save it.
Without logging in, every page, data request and image address sends you to the login page or is refused. This is tested automatically and by hand on the live address.
Records and images survive a redeploy and a restart.
Moved data matches your local copy (same record count and dashboard totals).
No secrets appear in the code, build logs or the pages sent to the browser. The AI key is only read on the server.

notes.title: The build plan in short
text: Build the full single-user billing app on your PC. Records can be added by hand or read from a photo of a slip or bill by Claude. Every record is converted to THB, and the app shows totals and charts, with a CSV export.
The work is sliced so each task delivers something you can see working. The riskiest unknown, how well Claude reads Thai slips, is tested in Task 2 before the app is built around it.
This plan covers Phase 1 only. Phase 2 (Railway) gets its own plan after Phase 1 passes.

notes.title: How the AI will build it
text: One AI agent works on one task at a time, in order. Tasks share files and one database layout, so working in parallel would cause conflicts.
After each task the checks run, the behaviour is confirmed by running it, and the work is saved with nothing sensitive included.
Review helpers look at the code at each checkpoint. A security review runs at Checkpoint D and at the end, and a test review runs at the end of Phase 1.
The AI stops and asks you first before real Claude calls, a new tool, a database change after the first version, or anything that makes the app reachable beyond your home network.

notes.title: Delivery in two phases
text: The work ships in two phases. Phase 2 starts only after Phase 1 meets its success criteria.

notes.title: Phase 1: run it on your PC
text: Every feature in this summary is built and runs on your PC, with phone access over your home network.
There is no login. Your data lives in a folder on your PC.
Phase 1 is done when its eight success criteria pass.

notes.title: Phase 2: put it online
text: The same app is put on your Railway account as a public web app with a secure address, so it works from your phone anywhere.
A login is added, and the app must not go public without it. Your data lives on a Railway storage volume.
No features change beyond what going online needs: the login, settings kept outside the code, a health check and moving your existing data.
Phase 2 is done when its five success criteria pass.

notes.title: How you use it in Phase 1
text: The app runs on your PC. To use the phone camera, the phone opens the app over your home network.
There is no login in this phase, so anyone on your home network can open it. Using it from outside your home is not part of this version.
The internet is needed for AI reading and exchange rates. Adding THB records by hand works offline.

notes.title: Going online in Phase 2
text: Railway is a hosting service. It builds the app from your code on GitHub, gives it a secure web address and keeps a storage volume, so your records and images survive updates.
One small service runs the app, with exactly one copy. The login is a single password that you set, with a 30-day sign-in, a limit on repeated wrong passwords and a logout button.
A one-time script moves your Phase 1 data to Railway, and the record counts and totals must match afterwards. The CSV export stays the main backup.
Railway charges by usage. You confirm the expected cost before anything is deployed.

risks.risk: Claude may misread Thai slips (amount, Buddhist-calendar date, income or spending).
risks.handling: Test on real slips before building around it. You always review before saving, and the instructions to Claude are tuned during that test.

risks.risk: iPhone HEIC photos may not be readable by the image tool.
risks.handling: iPhones usually convert to JPEG on upload. A real file is tested in Task 12. If that fails, a new tool is added after asking you.

risks.risk: The database tool may not install on Node 24 and Windows.
risks.handling: It is installed and tried first in Task 1. Fallback: use Node 22.

risks.risk: The exchange rate service may lack a currency or a weekend date.
risks.handling: Weekend dates use the previous working day's rate. An unsupported currency asks you to type a rate.

risks.risk: Windows Firewall may block your phone from reaching the app.
risks.handling: The README will describe the firewall rule.

risks.risk: Repeated real AI reading runs could cost money.
risks.handling: Real calls happen only through one manual command, each time with your approval. Automatic tests use a stand-in.

risks.risk: Real slips could leak into the public code repository.
risks.handling: Real samples stay in a folder the repository ignores, test samples are made up, and staged changes are checked before every upload.
